controls.rules_out: That any steering intervention, rather than ACT’s steering directions, produces the observed improvement.

controls.name: Single steering
controls.detail: An ablation using a single steering direction; the paper says this is consistent with ITI.
controls.rules_out: That ACT’s gains require only a single steering direction rather than its diverse steering mechanism.

controls.name: Adaptive intensity only
controls.detail: An ablation using Adaptive Steering Intensity Control without diverse steering.
controls.rules_out: That the full ACT result requires diverse steering in addition to adaptive intensity.

controls.name: Diverse steering only
controls.detail: An ablation using diverse probe-driven steering vectors with constant steering intensity.
controls.rules_out: That the full ACT result requires adaptive intensity in addition to diverse steering.

confounds.name: Automated GPT-judge scores may not reliably reflect truthfulness
confounds.detail: The original GPT-judge and GPT-info models used for TruthfulQA were retired, and the paper notes that using davinci-002 produces different metric values from prior work.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Human evaluations by a panel of ten experts are reported alongside GPT-judge scores to validate the assessment.

confounds.name: ACT may improve truthfulness by broadly changing the model’s output distribution
confounds.detail: A performance gain could reflect a large intervention-induced shift rather than a targeted truthfulness improvement.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper measures CE and KL deviation from the original generation distribution and reports them alongside truthfulness and informativeness metrics; it describes the gains as obtained with minimal intervention.

confounds.name: ACT may trade helpfulness or generated-text smoothness for truthfulness
confounds.detail: The authors explicitly note that truthfulness gains could affect helpfulness or the smoothness of generated text.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors state that this trade-off remains for future investigation.

evidence_standards.name: Two-fold cross-validation
evidence_standards.detail: The full-data TruthfulQA setting uses two-fold cross-validation, with 50% (408 samples) of the data for training.

evidence_standards.name: Probe train-validation split
evidence_standards.detail: Probe data are randomly split 4:1 into training and validation sets; validation accuracy is used to evaluate probes and select intervention heads.

evidence_standards.name: Human evaluation panel
evidence_standards.detail: Ten experts from diverse disciplines evaluate outputs; the paper reports human evaluation scores with ± values.

evidence_standards.name: Inference-time measurements
evidence_standards.detail: Inference time is averaged over three runs on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

datasets.name: Dictator Game
datasets.eval_protocol: In the altruism prompt study, 50 responses per game across five altruism-encouraging prefixes, five self-interest prefixes, and a no-prefix condition; the model chooses an amount to give from $0–$100 and gives a brief justification. For steering, multiple completions are sampled per coefficient, but the count is not specified. GPT-4.1-mini rates trait expression from 0–100 and extracts the amount given; no split is reported.

datasets.name: Trust Game
datasets.eval_protocol: In the altruism prompt study, 50 responses per game across five altruism-encouraging prefixes, five self-interest prefixes, and a no-prefix condition; Agent 1 chooses an amount from $0–$100 to send, and gives a brief justification. For steering, multiple completions are sampled per coefficient, but the count is not specified. GPT-4.1-mini rates trait expression from 0–100 and extracts the decision; no split is reported.

datasets.name: Ultimatum Game
datasets.eval_protocol: In the altruism prompt study, 50 responses per game across five altruism-encouraging prefixes, five self-interest prefixes, and a no-prefix condition; Agent 1 offers a split of $100 and gives a brief justification. For steering, multiple completions are sampled per coefficient, but the count is not specified. GPT-4.1-mini rates trait expression from 0–100 and extracts the offer; no split is reported.

datasets.name: Overfishing Game
datasets.eval_protocol: In the altruism prompt study, 50 responses per game across five altruism-encouraging prefixes, five self-interest prefixes, and a no-prefix condition; the model chooses a harvest from 0–100 fish and gives a brief justification. For steering, multiple completions are sampled per coefficient, but the count is not specified. GPT-4.1-mini rates trait expression from 0–100 and extracts the decision; no split is reported.

datasets.name: Prisoner's Dilemma
datasets.eval_protocol: In the altruism prompt study, 50 responses per game across five altruism-encouraging prefixes, five self-interest prefixes, and a no-prefix condition; the model chooses cooperate or defect and gives a brief justification. For steering, multiple completions are sampled per coefficient, but the count is not specified. GPT-4.1-mini rates trait expression from 0–100 and extracts the choice; no split is reported.

datasets.name: Apology Game
datasets.eval_protocol: In the altruism prompt study, 50 responses per game across five altruism-encouraging prefixes, five self-interest prefixes, and a no-prefix condition; after having caused Agent 2 to lose $100, Agent 1 chooses a transfer from $0–$100 and gives a brief justification. For steering, multiple completions are sampled per coefficient, but the count is not specified. GPT-4.1-mini rates trait expression from 0–100 and extracts the transfer; no split is reported.

datasets.name: Forgiveness game settings
datasets.eval_protocol: The paper evaluates a forgiveness vector on five games and eight total vignettes, including a Trust Game with prior betrayal, an iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, a costly punishment game, and a Dictator Game with partner selection. Steering is limited to |β|≤3 for coherence. GPT-4.1-mini rates forgiveness; strategic choices are also examined. No per-game trial counts or split are reported.

datasets.name: Expectations-of-others game vignettes
datasets.eval_protocol: The paper rewrites game vignettes so the model predicts another agent's behavior—for example, how much Agent 2 will give in a Dictator Game or whether Agent 2 will forgive a prior transgression. It evaluates expected-altruism and expected-forgiveness vectors; trial counts, split, and a detailed scoring protocol are not reported.

metrics.name: GPT-4.1-mini trait rating (0–100)
metrics.caveat: Ratings can track persuasive rhetoric without a corresponding strategic change, and can move opposite to strategic choices; the paper also reports extracted choices.

metrics.name: Layer-20 activation projection onto the persona vector
Extracted strategic choices (e.g., dollars shared or offered; cooperate/defect)
metrics.caveat: In forgiveness settings, choices can move opposite to GPT-rated forgiveness; the paper reports ratings alongside strategic choices.

metrics.name: Word occurrence frequency in justifications
metrics.caveat: Word use describes rhetoric and need not establish a corresponding strategic change; the paper also reports game decisions.

controls.name: No-steering condition (β=0)
controls.detail: The paper evaluates steering coefficients against β=0, the no-steering condition.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether observed outcomes differ from the model's unmodified behavior, rather than reflecting baseline behavior alone.

confounds.name: Steering changes rhetoric or judge impressions without changing strategy
confounds.detail: A model could sound more altruistic or forgiving and receive higher GPT ratings while making unchanged or less trait-consistent decisions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper extracts and reports concrete game decisions alongside GPT trait ratings; it finds cases where ratings and choices diverge.

confounds.name: Large steering coefficients degrade response coherence rather than cleanly steering the trait
confounds.detail: Reduced diversity, mismatches between reasoning and final choices, grandiose language, and occasional language switching could make extreme-coefficient results reflect off-distribution outputs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors inspect response coherence and focus most analyses on |β|≤3, while noting degradation at extreme values.

confounds.name: GPT-4.1-mini's shared biases or circularity drive the evaluations
confounds.detail: The same model is used for trait ratings and decision extraction, so shared judge biases could affect the reported results.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out by a separate measurement in this paper; the authors acknowledge this limitation and say human evaluation or alternative judges would strengthen the conclusions.

datasets.name: Anthropic Advanced AI Risk evaluation dataset
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for behavior-vector construction; steering is evaluated on 50 held-out multiple-choice questions in the same format. For open-ended evaluation, held-out questions are used without answer options.

datasets.name: Anthropic Sycophancy on NLP and Sycophancy on political typology
datasets.eval_protocol: Used together as the sycophancy data source for vector construction; steering is evaluated on 50 held-out multiple-choice questions and manually written open-ended questions.

datasets.name: GPT-4-generated Hallucination and Refusal contrastive datasets
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for vector construction; steering is evaluated on 50 held-out multiple-choice questions. For open-ended evaluation, held-out questions are adapted by removing the answer options.

datasets.name: MMLU
datasets.eval_protocol: Randomly sample 10 questions from each of 57 categories; reformat as A/B multiple-choice questions with the correct answer’s letter randomized; report average probability assigned to the correct answer.

datasets.name: TruthfulQA
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to assess the effect of subtracting the sycophancy vector; the paper refers to full results in Appendix H but does not specify the evaluation protocol here.

datasets.name: Open-ended behavioral questions
datasets.eval_protocol: For sycophancy, use manually written questions; for other behaviors, adapt held-out multiple-choice questions by keeping only the initial question. GPT-4 rates responses from 1 to 10 for the behavior being evaluated; results are averaged over 50 prompts.

baselines.name: System prompting
baselines.fair_comparison: Compare positive and negative behavior-specific system prompts with CAA on the same behavioral evaluations; the paper tests CAA together with prompting. It reports trying several prompt options but does not fully optimize the prompting baseline.

baselines.name: Supervised finetuning
baselines.fair_comparison: Finetune Llama 2 7B Chat on the same multiple-choice datasets used for CAA, for one epoch with SGD and learning rate 1×10⁻⁴; evaluate on the held-out test questions and open-ended tasks. The paper acknowledges that finetuning hyperparameters were not optimized.

baselines.name: Few-shot prompting
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper says initial experiments found it less effective than system prompting, but gives no further comparison protocol.

metrics.name: GPT-4 open-ended behavioral score (1–10)
metrics.caveat: Scores can be sensitive to scoring-prompt wording and may reflect LLM biases that differ from human judgments; the authors manually inspect a sample of ratings against their own manual scores.

metrics.name: MMLU average probability assigned to the correct answer
Cosine similarity between steering vectors and per-token activations, or between steering vectors from different layers/models

controls.name: Zero steering multiplier (unmodified model)
controls.detail: Evaluate with multiplier 0 alongside positive and negative steering multipliers.
controls.rules_out: That the reported behavioral change is simply the model’s unmodified behavior.

confounds.name: Behavioral score changes reflect general capability damage rather than targeted behavior steering
confounds.detail: A model with broadly degraded capabilities could change its behavioral answers without the targeted behavior being represented or controlled.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate interventions on MMLU and, for sycophancy steering, TruthfulQA; the paper reports that MMLU performance is not significantly affected and that subtracting the sycophancy vector slightly improves TruthfulQA performance.

confounds.name: Behavioral changes are an artifact of degraded or low-quality generations
confounds.detail: Poor-quality generations could receive different behavioral scores without demonstrating useful targeted steering.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors assess larger-multiplier text quality using GPT-4 and human readers, report degradation at larger multipliers, and limit the multiplier range to balance steering with generation quality.

confounds.name: GPT-4 evaluator artifacts account for open-ended results
confounds.detail: GPT-4 ratings may vary with prompt wording or reflect evaluator biases rather than the behavior displayed by the response.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Manually inspect a sample of GPT-4 ratings and compare them with the authors’ own manual scores; the paper says these correspond well, while acknowledging the evaluator limitations.

confounds.name: Weak baseline optimization exaggerates CAA’s advantage over prompting or finetuning
confounds.detail: More effective system prompts or better-tuned finetuning could reduce the measured advantage of CAA.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the authors acknowledge that they did not exhaustively optimize prompting and did not optimize finetuning hyperparameters; they note that better baselines could yield smaller CAA effects.

datasets.name: Persona datasets (Perez et al., 2023)
datasets.eval_protocol: 26 multiple-choice datasets; each is split 50-50, with the train split used to construct the steering vector and compute separation metrics and the test split used to compute steerability.

datasets.name: Truthfulness datasets (Ying et al., 2026)
datasets.eval_protocol: 5 datasets; each is split 50-50, with the train split used to construct the steering vector and compute separation metrics and the test split used to compute steerability.

datasets.name: Safety datasets (Zhang et al., 2024)
datasets.eval_protocol: 7 datasets; each is split 50-50, with the train split used to construct the steering vector and compute separation metrics and the test split used to compute steerability.

metrics.name: Steerability
metrics.caveat: It is evaluated on multiple-choice option logits; the paper does not test whether it corresponds to fluent free-form generation or whether steering harms fluency or unrelated-task performance.

metrics.name: Intrinsic dimension
metrics.caveat: It is weak overall, varies by dataset family, and its correlation drops markedly when controlling for layers.

confounds.name: Dataset and layer effects explain the separation–steerability correlations
confounds.detail: The observed correlations could reflect which dataset or intervention layer is used rather than a general relationship between separation and steerability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compute partial correlations after linear residualization on dataset or layer indicator variables; the correlations remain, including for SNR.

confounds.name: An unknown third variable causes both feature recovery and steerability
confounds.detail: The reported association could arise without separation or feature recovery contributing to steerability; the authors explicitly say this possibility remains open.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper identifies this as a limitation and does not measure or control for the unknown variable.

confounds.name: Steering improves the multiple-choice score while degrading fluency or other capabilities
confounds.detail: The headline option-logit change could occur alongside worse free-form fluency or performance on unrelated tasks.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the authors say they do not test free-form fluency or unrelated-task performance.

evidence_standards.name: Statistical significance threshold
evidence_standards.detail: Correlations are treated as statistically significant at p < 0.05; Table 1 marks exceptions, and the paper reports Pearson r and Spearman ρ. No seed or repeated-run standard is specified.

datasets.name: ESD (English subset)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the official partition: 300 training, 20 development, and 30 test utterances; all speaker–emotion variants of an utterance are kept in the same split. Objective evaluation is on synthesized test speech: Whisper-Large-v3 for WER, WavLM-Base for speaker similarity, DNSMOS for perceived quality, and emotion2vec for emotion recognition. Subjective evaluation uses 25 balanced utterances (5 per emotion) for MOS and Emo-MOS.

baselines.name: CosyVoice-SFT
baselines.fair_comparison: A fully fine-tuned version of the CosyVoice backbone; further comparison details are not stated.

baselines.name: CosyVoice-SFT-Shift
baselines.fair_comparison: The EmoSteer layer is inserted and fine-tuned on top of fully fine-tuned CosyVoice; further comparison details are not stated.

metrics.name: MOS
metrics.caveat: Rates overall audio quality and naturalness on a five-point scale.

metrics.name: Emo-MOS
metrics.caveat: Rates whether speech conveys the intended emotion, not how closely the expression matches the ground truth; reported alongside MOS.

controls.name: EmoSteer-absent versions of the same base models
controls.detail: Human preference tests compare versions with and without EmoSteer for both CosyVoice and CosyVoice-SFT.
controls.rules_out: A preference gain attributable only to the choice of base model, rather than adding EmoSteer.

controls.name: Models without EmoSteer across steering-factor settings
controls.detail: The paper compares emotion recognition accuracy for models with and without EmoSteer as the inference steering factor varies.
controls.rules_out: That the reported advantage across steering settings is present without the EmoSteer layer; the paper notes an exception at α=4.

confounds.name: Higher emotion-recognition accuracy may not correspond to perceptually stronger emotional expression
confounds.detail: An accuracy change from the emotion2vec SER evaluator could occur without listeners perceiving stronger expression.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper also runs human AB preference tests on emotional intensity, asking listeners to choose which of paired versions has the stronger perceived expression.

evidence_standards.name: MOS and Emo-MOS listener study
evidence_standards.detail: 10 listeners rate 25 utterances, balanced across emotions with 5 samples per emotion. Scores are reported with 95% confidence intervals computed using a t-test over listener ratings.

evidence_standards.name: Human preference tests
evidence_standards.detail: 10 listeners participate in preference tests; results are reported as win rates. For the intensity AB test, 5 utterances are randomly sampled per emotion, versions at α=1 to 3 in 0.5 increments are generated, and adjacent versions are paired.

datasets.name: HarmBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Safety/control evaluation; the provided text does not specify the split, episode or trial count, scoring rule, or preprocessing.

datasets.name: MMLU-Pro
datasets.eval_protocol: Used to measure capability with accuracy; the provided text does not specify the split, trial count, or preprocessing.

datasets.name: MATH-500
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for IF-Boxed and IF-Plain formatting tasks; capability is measured with MATH-500 accuracy. The provided text does not specify the split, trial count, or preprocessing.

baselines.name: full steering
baselines.fair_comparison: Duration comparisons use the same layer and direction and start at the final input token; the text does not specify further matching details.

baselines.name: prompting
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the evaluated models and tasks; the text does not specify further matching details.

baselines.name: linear decay
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with Prefix Steering on OLMo 3 7B across the evaluated tasks; further matching details are not stated.

baselines.name: exponential decay
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with Prefix Steering on OLMo 3 7B across the evaluated tasks; further matching details are not stated.

baselines.name: DAS
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with Prefix Steering on OLMo 3 7B across the evaluated tasks; further matching details are not stated.

baselines.name: ACT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with Prefix Steering on OLMo 3 7B across the evaluated tasks; further matching details are not stated.

metrics.name: behavioral control / target-behavior success
metrics.caveat: Control alone does not show the capability cost; the paper reports it alongside capability accuracy and compares control–capability trade-offs.

metrics.name: MMLU-Pro accuracy
metrics.caveat: Capability accuracy alone does not show behavioral control; the paper reports it alongside control.

metrics.name: MATH-500 accuracy
metrics.caveat: Capability accuracy alone does not show behavioral control; the paper reports it alongside control.

metrics.name: attention-output error
metrics.caveat: An attention-level match does not determine behavioral control or capability effects during generation; the paper also evaluates behavioral control and capability.

metrics.name: dimension of the matching subspace (dim U-perp)

controls.name: unsteered model
controls.detail: The paper includes the unsteered model alongside steering conditions in the control–capability evaluations.
controls.rules_out: That the reported control–capability result is simply the unmodified model’s behavior.

controls.name: random projected-space perturbations
controls.detail: For the attention-output error experiment, perturbations to W_Q h are sampled from the full projected space and compared with perturbations in U, the directions described as sensitive.
controls.rules_out: That the error pattern is specific to the theoretically sensitive directions rather than also appearing for the random projected-space comparison.

evidence_standards.name: Attention-output experiment reporting
evidence_standards.detail: For the reported attention-output analyses, figures show means and sample standard deviations; the paper states that the relevant results use 100 examples. No statistical test, seed-based criterion, or explicit threshold for treating differences as real is specified.

datasets.name: Q₈ finite-group state-tracking task
datasets.eval_protocol: The model reports running states for moves in Q₈. On held-out items, edit the current hidden-bit token and score the predicted next hidden bit on the discriminating subset where the edited-state and original-state transitions differ; report register agreement and Counterfactual Update Selectivity. The central evaluation item count and split size are not stated.

datasets.name: D₈ finite-group state-tracking task
datasets.eval_protocol: The model reports running states for moves in D₈. On held-out items, edit the current hidden-bit token and score the predicted next hidden bit on the discriminating subset where the edited-state and original-state transitions differ; report register agreement and Counterfactual Update Selectivity. The central evaluation item count and split size are not stated.

datasets.name: Present-to-past conversion
datasets.eval_protocol: Qwen, intervention at block 7 with coefficient 15, selected on separate calibration data; evaluate on 64 new prompts not used for construction or calibration. Compare target-minus-alternative log-probability margin changes against the repeated correct-prompt patch reference.

datasets.name: English-to-Spanish translation
datasets.eval_protocol: Llama, intervention at block 8 with coefficient 10, selected on separate calibration data; evaluate on 64 new prompts not used for construction or calibration. The described prompt construction uses ten input-output demonstrations; shuffled prompts retain the inputs, output set, and query while permuting demonstration outputs. Compare target-minus-alternative log-probability margin changes against the repeated correct-prompt patch reference.

baselines.name: Function Vector (FV) steering
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper compares FV steering with counterfactual register editing in the Q₈ task and with target-prompt patching in the lexical-task experiments. For the lexical comparisons, task, layer, and steering strength are selected on separate calibration data, and interventions are evaluated on the same 64 new prompts per model.

metrics.name: Register agreement (R)
metrics.caveat: Agreement with the counterfactual next state alone does not measure preference over the original next state; the paper reports CUS alongside it.

metrics.name: Counterfactual Update Selectivity (CUS)
metrics.caveat: Reports preference for the edited-state transition over the original-state transition on the discriminating subset; the paper uses additional move-swap and conflicting-continuation selectivities to test whether this reflects applying the operation to a state rather than supplying an answer.

metrics.name: Held-out linear-readout accuracy
metrics.caveat: Decodability does not establish causal use; the paper distinguishes it from the causal register-editing tests.

metrics.name: Normalized effect (E)
metrics.caveat: The paper says this compares behavioral effects, not hidden-vector similarity.

metrics.name: Target-minus-alternative log-probability margin
metrics.caveat: A behavioral margin gain alone does not establish that steering recreates the natural target activation or writes a state-like value; the paper compares it with patching and natural-scale steering.

metrics.name: Cosine similarity between FV and register-write updates
FV energy in the rank-16 register subspace
Norm ratio of steering vector to median natural activation change
metrics.caveat: The paper treats a successful effect at a much larger-than-natural displacement as evidence that steering need not reproduce the natural target activation at that site; it also tests natural-scale steering.

controls.name: Random-subspace edit
controls.detail: Apply a same-rank edit in a random subspace at the current-state token.
controls.rules_out: That an edit of the same rank, merely because an intervention occurred, redirects the computation.

controls.name: Orthogonal-complement edit
controls.detail: Apply a same-rank edit within the orthogonal complement of the identified register subspace.
controls.rules_out: That a same-rank edit outside the identified register redirects the computation.

controls.name: Full-residual replacement
controls.detail: Replace the entire current-state-token residual with the counterfactual class mean.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the rank-16 register edit is weaker than replacing the whole residual; the paper reports that full replacement is no stronger.

controls.name: Move-swap control
controls.detail: Hold the edited state fixed and vary the upcoming move; score whether the predicted next state changes with that move.
controls.rules_out: That the intervention merely supplies a fixed answer rather than a state used with the current operation.

controls.name: Conflicting-continuation control
controls.detail: Inject a real occurrence of the counterfactual state whose own continuation conflicts with the transition under the current move.
controls.rules_out: That the model copies a supplied continuation instead of computing from the edited state and current move.

controls.name: Single real occurrence of the counterfactual state
controls.detail: Use an actual occurrence of the counterfactual state as well as the constructed counterfactual edit.
controls.rules_out: That the effect depends on constructing or averaging a counterfactual state.

controls.name: Matched visible-coordinate localization control
controls.detail: Route a candidate component from the visible coordinate rather than the hidden coordinate; the study also uses restoration of the component contribution from the clean edited run.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether localization depends on the hidden-coordinate route rather than a matched visible-coordinate route; restoration tests recovery of the removed contribution.

controls.name: One-block correct-prompt patch
controls.detail: Replace the shuffled-run final-token activation with the matched correct-prompt activation at the selected block once, then let later blocks proceed normally.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the natural target activation at the intervention site is locally sufficient for the target behavior.

controls.name: Natural-scale mean steering
controls.detail: Rescale the Function Vector to the norm of the matched correct-versus-shuffled activation change.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether steering remains effective at the scale of the natural activation change rather than only at the calibrated, much larger scale.

controls.name: Same-norm comparison directions
controls.detail: Compare the task FV with the prompt-specific correct-minus-shuffled direction, a held-out average of that direction, another task’s FV, and a random direction, each rescaled to the task FV’s norm.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the effect is specific to the learned task direction rather than being explained by direction-independent scale; the paper finds specificity differs by model.

controls.name: Unedited shuffled prompt
controls.detail: Use the shuffled prompt without an intervention as the reference for intervention-induced margin changes.
controls.rules_out: Provides the no-intervention reference for the measured behavioral gain.

controls.name: Progressive downstream vector subtraction
controls.detail: Add the FV at its usual layer and subtract it at progressively later layers.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the early steering pulse has become a self-sustaining task state independent of the ongoing perturbation.

controls.name: Output-label remapping
controls.detail: Hold the underlying task fixed while remapping output labels, and test whether steering reverses with the new mapping.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the steering effect tracks the abstract correct answer rather than remaining tied partly to the same literal label.

confounds.name: The trace value is decodable but not causally used
confounds.detail: A readable hidden-bit token could be present without later computation using it as state.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Edit the hidden-bit coordinate and measure whether the next-state prediction follows the transition from the edited value; also report register agreement and CUS.

confounds.name: The register edit merely pushes a fixed answer
confounds.detail: A changed next-state answer could occur without the model applying the actual upcoming operation to the edited state.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Move-swap selectivity: vary the move while holding the edited state fixed and test whether the predicted next state changes accordingly.

confounds.name: The model copies a continuation associated with an injected state
confounds.detail: The apparent counterfactual result could come from copying a continuation already associated with the supplied state.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Inject a real counterfactual-state occurrence with a conflicting continuation and compare whether the model follows that continuation or the current move applied to the state.

confounds.name: The state-edit effect is an artifact of constructing or averaging the counterfactual
confounds.detail: The result might depend on the construction of the counterfactual rather than the state value itself.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Test a single real occurrence of the counterfactual state; the paper reports it is as effective as the constructed counterfactual.

confounds.name: Successful FV steering directly writes the identified register
confounds.detail: Behavioral success could be interpreted as the FV writing the same causal register identified in the state-tracking task.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On held-out examples, compare the FV update with the matched register write: measure update size, cosine similarity, and the fraction of FV energy in the rank-16 register subspace. The paper finds a larger, mostly out-of-subspace update, while noting that another register or a distributed representation remains possible.

confounds.name: FV success reflects restoration of the model’s natural target activation
confounds.detail: The target behavior could result from reconstructing the activation naturally produced by the correct prompt.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Patch the matched correct-prompt activation once at the selected block and separately rescale the FV to the natural correct-versus-shuffled activation-change norm; both have little effect compared with the repeated target patch or calibrated FV.

confounds.name: The FV effect is explained by magnitude alone
confounds.detail: Because calibrated FVs are much larger than natural activation changes, their effects might be due only to their norm.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare equal-norm task and comparison directions. Llama is selective among tested directions; Qwen also responds to several structured comparison directions, so specificity is model-dependent.

confounds.name: The FV acts as an abstract correct-answer signal
confounds.detail: Steering could encode the abstract correct answer rather than task computation, or could remain tied to a literal answer label.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Remap output labels while holding the underlying task fixed: the unedited models follow the new mapping, but the steering effect does not reverse with it.

confounds.name: The steering pulse quickly becomes a self-sustaining task state
confounds.detail: The initial perturbation might be converted downstream into an independent state that continues to drive the task.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Subtract the vector at progressively later layers; early subtraction eliminates the task-specific effect, with effects surviving only when subtraction is delayed until late layers.

confounds.name: The target-task representation is distributed or constructed downstream rather than locally sufficient at the tested site
confounds.detail: The one-block patch’s failure need not mean there is no natural target state elsewhere or across multiple activations; the authors explicitly leave these possibilities open.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the one-block patch tests local sufficiency only at the selected site, and the paper states that representations elsewhere, distributed across activations, or constructed downstream remain possible.

evidence_standards.name: 95% bootstrap intervals for held-out register tests
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports 95% bootstrap intervals on held-out items and says the intervals for the summarized causal selectivity tests exclude zero.

evidence_standards.name: Paired 95% bootstrap intervals for lexical-task intervention effects
evidence_standards.detail: Intervals are computed from 2,000 paired resamples; results are reported under the calibrated settings on new prompts.

evidence_standards.name: Multiple reported splits for D₈ localization
evidence_standards.detail: The frozen four-edge route is reported across ten splits, eight of which are held-out confirmatory splits.

datasets.name: PopQA

metrics.name: Detection rate
metrics.caveat: A high rate alone can reflect always claiming an injection; the paper reports false-positive rate on clean inputs alongside it.

metrics.name: Concept identification rate
metrics.caveat: Text-based context priming can mislead identification; the paper reports identification under adversarial prompts and context priming alongside the main result.

metrics.name: Steering success rate
metrics.caveat: At high steering strengths, base-model outputs can become incoherent, affecting the comparison; the paper reports that 55% of Qwen 2.5 32B base responses are incoherent at α = 32.

metrics.name: Compliance rate
metrics.caveat: The adapted model has elevated compliance even without steering, so the paper reports the unsteered base and adapted rates alongside the steered comparison.

metrics.name: MMLU performance
metrics.caveat: Capability performance changes alongside detection; the paper reports detection and MMLU performance together across LoRA scales.

metrics.name: GSM8K performance
metrics.caveat: Capability performance changes alongside detection; the paper reports detection and GSM8K performance together across LoRA scales.

metrics.name: Cosine similarity to the CAA direction
metrics.caveat: Detection depends on directional alignment, so extraction-method results are reported alongside cosine similarity rather than detection alone.

metrics.name: Held-out cosine similarity of the predicted perturbation
metrics.caveat: A scaling-only predictor is also reported, to distinguish affine rotation from merely scaling the injected vector.

controls.name: Clean, no-injection inputs
controls.detail: Evaluate clean inputs and measure spurious injection reports.
controls.rules_out: That detection performance is explained by the model always claiming an injection.

controls.name: Norm-matched random Gaussian noise
controls.detail: Inject random Gaussian vectors matched in L2 norm to concept vectors; also use norm-matched noise in the layer-41 causal injection test.
controls.rules_out: That detection is merely a response to perturbation magnitude or generic anomalous activation changes.

controls.name: Adversarial prompt with a mismatched concept
controls.detail: Inject concept A while the prompt suggests concept B.
controls.rules_out: That the reported concept is determined only by the prompt rather than the injected activation; the model correctly identifies the injected concept in 89% of cases.

controls.name: Text-based context priming
controls.detail: Inject concept A while system context primes concept B.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether textual evidence alone determines the report; the 70% identification result shows this rival cue can still mislead the detector.

controls.name: Random direction
controls.detail: Evaluate a random direction as an alternative vector direction in the extraction-method comparison.
controls.rules_out: That any direction produces detection; the random direction has approximately zero detection.

controls.name: Raw steering vector injected directly at layer 41
controls.detail: Inject the original vector at layer 41, bypassing intermediate layers, and compare its detection probability with the affine-predicted perturbation.
controls.rules_out: That the raw injected vector alone is sufficient to explain detection at the final layer.

controls.name: Base model with LoRA disabled
controls.detail: Compare the unadapted model with the detection-trained model in detection and resistance evaluations.
controls.rules_out: That the reported detection or change in steering susceptibility is present to the same extent without detection fine-tuning.

controls.name: Injection layer-depth ablation
controls.detail: Train and evaluate at 25%, 50%, 67%, and 83% of model depth.
controls.rules_out: That the reported detection result is independent of where the intervention is injected.

controls.name: Injection token-position ablation
controls.detail: For Gemma 2 9B at layer 28, inject at the first, middle, or last prompt token.
controls.rules_out: That detection depends only on using the last prompt-token position.

controls.name: Head ablations
controls.detail: Ablate heads and measure the effect on detection rate.
controls.rules_out: That a small coalition of attention heads is necessary for the detector.

confounds.name: Generic anomaly detection rather than detection of semantic steering content
confounds.detail: A detector might report any unusual activation perturbation as steering, without recognizing the injected concept.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Test norm-matched Gaussian noise and concept A injected with a prompt suggesting concept B; noise is rejected 94% of the time and the actual injected concept is correctly identified 89% of the time.

confounds.name: Textual cues, rather than the activation, determine the reported concept
confounds.detail: The prompt or system context could name a concept and drive the model's report independently of the injected vector.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Use mismatched prompts and context priming. The model identifies the actually injected concept in 89% of adversarial-prompt cases, but context priming reduces identification to 70%, so this explanation is not fully ruled out.

confounds.name: Detection transfer reflects vector magnitude or extraction method rather than geometric alignment
confounds.detail: Alternative vectors might transfer simply because of their norms or their extraction procedure, rather than because their directions align with the CAA training distribution.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Rescale alternative-method vectors to the mean CAA norm and measure cosine similarity to CAA; detection tracks alignment (reported r > 0.9), while low-alignment methods have approximately zero detection.

confounds.name: Increased steering success is an artifact of base-model incoherence at high steering strength
confounds.detail: Base models may fail to produce targeted answers because strong steering makes their outputs garbled or off-topic, rather than because adapted models are more susceptible.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure incoherent base-model responses; for Qwen 2.5 32B at α = 32, 55% are incoherent. This documents the rival explanation but does not fully rule it out.

confounds.name: Higher safety-benchmark compliance is caused by fine-tuning degradation, not awareness enabling or failing to resist steering
confounds.detail: Detection training itself may weaken refusal behavior, so elevated compliance under steering need not reflect a failure to use detected intervention information.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report compliance without steering: 23% for the adapted model versus 1% for the base model. The paper treats this as evidence of degraded safety alignment from fine-tuning, not as a ruled-out explanation.

evidence_standards.name: Five random seeds for the held-out-concept detection results
evidence_standards.detail: Detection rates are averaged over five random seeds, with ± values reported in the results table; the paper does not specify what dispersion measure ± denotes.

evidence_standards.name: Dual-judge classification
evidence_standards.detail: Responses are classified using keyword regex plus GPT-4o-mini, with reported inter-judge agreement above 99%.

metrics.name: Top-1 token prediction accuracy
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that a reduction in top-1 coding accuracy may not translate into a reduction in real-world risk from coding ability; it reports text accuracy alongside code/Python accuracy to track alignment tax.

metrics.name: Matching score
metrics.caveat: Invalid answers and mode collapse can make the score misleading as a measure of behavioural preference. The paper discards settings with more than 5% faulty output tokens or with either valid answer above 95% frequency; for combined steering it assigns scores of -0.1 for too many faulty answers and -0.2 for mode collapse. It also notes that the relation between matching scores and real or open-ended performance remains uncertain.

controls.name: Permuted steering vectors
controls.detail: For each steering vector, permute activations per layer, preserving the mean and standard deviation while changing their order; the paper says this changes activations by the same total amount as the original vector.
controls.rules_out: Whether the effect depends on the original ordering of the steering-vector activations rather than merely changing activations by a comparable amount.

controls.name: Unsteered model
controls.detail: Use normal model behaviour as the reference: injection coefficient 0 for broad steering, and the default matching score for behavioural steering.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported change is present relative to the model's normal, unmodified behaviour.

confounds.name: Broad coding-steering effects reflect similar distortion of the model rather than a broad-skill direction
confounds.detail: The similar results for broad coding and narrower Python steering could arise because the two steering vectors distort the model's workings to a similar extent.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper examines activation-distribution spread in Appendix C and notes that Python activations have a smaller spread than general-coding activations at layer 15; it also uses the same injection coefficients, which it says rules out coefficient size as the explanation.

confounds.name: Python results are correlated with general coding because Python made up a large part of Llama 2's coding training data
confounds.detail: If Python constituted a large share of the model's coding data, similar Python and general-coding steering results would not establish that broad steering works independently of the narrower skill.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not resolved: the authors say Llama 2's training data is private and propose experiments removing programming languages other than Python as future work.

confounds.name: The apparent behavioural change is general model impairment or mode collapse, not a behavioural preference
confounds.detail: A model that cannot answer the questions properly, or that nearly always emits one option, can produce misleading matching scores without exhibiting the target behaviour.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Discard hyperparameters when more than 5% of output tokens are invalid or either valid answer occurs more than 95% of the time; combined steering also receives designated penalties for faulty answers and mode collapse.

confounds.name: Simultaneous steering loses efficacy through interactions between injections at different layers
confounds.detail: Steering at one layer changes the activations encountered by steering at another layer, potentially reducing or altering the effects.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure matching scores under simultaneous steering and compare them with the individual-steering results; the authors report that interaction effects do not substantially reduce the effects for myopia and wealth seeking, while noting weaker or unstable results for other behaviours.

confounds.name: Matching-score changes may not reflect real or open-ended behaviour, or a reduction in risk
confounds.detail: A change in the binary-question score may not correspond to the model's behaviour in open-ended generation or to a meaningful reduction in real-world risk.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not resolved by this paper's experiments; it cites prior work indicating that matching can translate to open-ended generation, but acknowledges that the relation to real performance and risk remains unclear.

LM-judge metrics use AlpacaEval instructions. Less costly metrics use all 500 concepts and costlier metrics use a shared 50-concept subset; the prompt count is not stated.

baselines.name: Prompt Steering
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same models, tasks, and evaluation examples as other methods; the paper compares methods across steering-factor sweeps and reports efficacy–side-effect trade-offs.

baselines.name: Simple Prompt Steering
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same models, tasks, and evaluation examples as other methods; the paper compares methods across steering-factor sweeps and reports efficacy–side-effect trade-offs.

baselines.name: LoRA
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same models, tasks, and evaluation examples as other methods; the paper compares methods across steering-factor sweeps and reports efficacy–side-effect trade-offs.

baselines.name: SFT
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated under the shared comparison protocol, but trained and evaluated on 20 concepts rather than the full 500-concept setting.

metrics.name: IFEval strict instruction-following accuracy
metrics.caveat: Reported as an independent side-effect metric and excluded from Overall.

metrics.name: JailbreakBench jailbreak and refusal behavior (including ASR and FRR)
metrics.caveat: Risk-oriented metrics are reversed before computing side-effect deltas (for example, 1-ASR and 1-FRR).

metrics.name: BBQ ambiguous and disambiguated bias scores
metrics.caveat: Signed bias scores are converted using their negative absolute values before computing side-effect deltas.

metrics.name: Overall
metrics.caveat: The harmonic mean of Concept Expression, Instruction Relevance, and Fluency is zero if any constituent is zero; it is used for factor selection and Method Properties, not as an additional metric in the 15-metric suite.

metrics.name: Side-effect delta
metrics.caveat: Absolute performance can obscure change relative to the unsteered model, so the paper reports both absolute steered-model performance and change against the unsteered base on the same prompts.

metrics.name: Composite side effects
metrics.caveat: An aggregate can obscure metric-specific differences: method rankings vary across individual side-effect metrics. The paper also checks robustness to alternative metric weightings.

metrics.name: Cross-Lingual Retention
metrics.caveat: Absolute scores can reflect differences in the unsteered model across languages, so retention is based on improvements relative to the language-matched unsteered model.

metrics.name: Sample Efficiency
metrics.caveat: Absolute task scores make data-efficiency comparisons across methods difficult; the paper normalizes reduced-data improvement by the corresponding full-data improvement.

metrics.name: Concept Gain
metrics.caveat: Compared across ID and OOD prompts as a base-relative gain, rather than relying on absolute scores.

metrics.name: Instruction Degradation
metrics.caveat: Measured relative to the language-matched unsteered model; positive degradation indicates worse performance.

metrics.name: Fluency Degradation
metrics.caveat: Measured relative to the language-matched unsteered model; positive degradation indicates worse performance.

controls.name: Random
controls.detail: Applies DiffMean after randomly partitioning the training examples, removing concept-specific label alignment.
controls.rules_out: Whether the effect requires concept-specific label alignment rather than merely applying a DiffMean intervention.

controls.name: Unsteered base model
controls.detail: Side-effect performance is compared with the unsteered base model on the same prompts; language-shift comparisons use a language-matched unsteered model.
controls.rules_out: Whether observed changes are present without steering, and whether cross-language score differences reflect the base model rather than steering.

controls.name: Reversed steering direction
controls.detail: The paper reverses the steering direction and checks whether low-strength off-target improvements are removed or reversed.
controls.rules_out: Whether low-strength gains are a generic effect of weak perturbations rather than direction-dependent conceptual entanglement.

confounds.name: Cross-language differences in the unsteered model could account for apparent retention differences
confounds.detail: Absolute scores across languages can differ because the base model performs differently in each language, even without steering.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure base-relative improvements using the language-matched unsteered model and calculate OOD retention as the OOD-to-ID ratio of those gains.

confounds.name: Low-strength off-target gains could result from generic weak perturbations rather than conceptual entanglement
confounds.detail: If any weak intervention produced the gains, they would not establish a direction-dependent steering effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reverse the steering direction; the reported gains are removed or reversed.

confounds.name: Selecting a steering factor on the full in-distribution evaluation set could make operating-point results optimistic
confounds.detail: The paper acknowledges that selecting the factor on the full ID evaluation set may introduce optimism in calibration.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For Generalization and Data Dependence experiments, select one method-level factor and hold it fixed without using OOD-language or reduced-data outcomes; the paper does not claim this removes optimism from the ID calibration itself.

datasets.name: Author-constructed dual-stance item set
datasets.eval_protocol: 50 items across 25 topics and four content categories, with two contradictory stances per topic. Topics were split with stratification and at least two test topics per category; training items were used to compute the steering direction and test items for held-out evaluation. Main steering test used 20 trials per item at temperature 0.9. Agreement was parsed using a three-stage YES/NO and phrase-matching procedure and reported as agreement rate.

datasets.name: 12-topic out-of-sample set
datasets.eval_protocol: 12 novel topics spanning expected-sycophantic, expected-opinionated, and intermediate items. Dual-stance consistency was measured at baseline; steering susceptibility was predicted using the regression fit on the original 25 topics and evaluated with 15 trials per item-stance at α=2.0. Predicted versus actual effects were compared with Pearson and Spearman correlations.

metrics.name: Agreement rate
metrics.caveat: Single-stance agreement cannot distinguish sycophancy from a stable model preference, and floor effects can make steering look specific; the paper tests both contradictory stances per topic.

metrics.name: Steering effect magnitude (agreement reduction)
metrics.caveat: Differential headroom could make larger-baseline items appear more susceptible; the paper compares sycophantic and factual items with similar baseline agreement.

metrics.name: Dual-stance consistency (minimum of the two stance-wise agreement rates)
metrics.caveat: The paper notes it may proxy for shallowness of agreement rather than sycophancy directly, and has a floor effect when minimum agreement is zero; it also tests prediction on 12 novel topics.

metrics.name: Pearson correlation
metrics.caveat: Dual-stance consistency may proxy for shallowness rather than sycophancy; the paper also reports Spearman correlation and tests the relationship out of sample.

metrics.name: Spearman correlation
metrics.caveat: The paper reports it alongside Pearson correlation and tests prediction on novel topics.

metrics.name: Response validity
metrics.caveat: Used alongside mean response length to check that agreement changes in the coherent-generation regime were not output collapse.

metrics.name: Mean response length
metrics.caveat: Used alongside response validity to check that agreement changes in the coherent-generation regime were not output collapse.

metrics.name: Grassmann similarity
metrics.caveat: The paper compares the sycophantic/factual activation split against random partitions of agree activations.

metrics.name: Steering-direction projection onto activation subspaces (projection ratio)

controls.name: Unsteered condition (α=0)
controls.detail: The same evaluation items were run without adding the steering vector, alongside steered conditions.
controls.rules_out: Provides the reference agreement rates against which steering effects are measured.

controls.name: Random-direction control
controls.detail: A random direction was tested on a subset of items; its differential was 7.3%, compared with 74.6% for the real direction.
controls.rules_out: That the structured differential susceptibility is a general consequence of applying any perturbation.

controls.name: Steering-strength sweep
controls.detail: The paper swept α from 0 to 2.0, with α=4.0 also tested; it monitored agreement, response validity, and response length.
controls.rules_out: That the observed dissociation is an artefact of one chosen steering strength; validity and length also expose output collapse at high strength.

controls.name: Neutral and expert prompt framings
controls.detail: The same diagnostic items were tested under neutral and expert prompts as well as the casual-friend framing, with baseline and steered conditions at 10 trials per item-stance and α=1.0; the same vector trained on casual-frame activations was used.
controls.rules_out: That the sycophancy classification or steering non-specificity depends only on the original casual-friend framing.

controls.name: Random partitions of agree activations
controls.detail: The sycophantic/factual subspace alignment was compared with the distribution from 500 random splits of agree activations.
controls.rules_out: That the observed subspace distinctness is an ordinary result of splitting agree activations into groups.

confounds.name: Differential headroom from different baseline agreement rates
confounds.detail: A larger reduction on sycophantic items might arise simply because their agreement rates leave more room to fall.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Sycophantic items had 93.2% baseline agreement and hard-fact correct stances 95.7%, yet mean reductions were 88.9% and 14.3%, respectively.

confounds.name: Any perturbation, rather than the semantic content of the steering direction, causes the differential effect
confounds.detail: The headline differential might reflect a generic effect of perturbing the residual stream.
confounds.ruled_out_by: A random-direction control on a subset produced a 7.3% differential versus 74.6% for the real direction.

confounds.name: Output collapse or incoherent generation explains reduced agreement
confounds.detail: Steering could lower agreement because responses become invalid or systematically shorter rather than because behaviour changes coherently.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For α≤2.0, validity remained above 88% and mean response length showed no systematic decline; validity fell below 68% at α=4.0, which the paper identifies as output collapse.

confounds.name: The result is specific to the casual-friend prompt framing
confounds.detail: The apparent sycophancy or non-specificity might be produced only by the social-compliance prompt context.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Under neutral and expert framings, baseline sycophantic agreement was 5% and 2%; under neutral framing, steering still reduced hard-fact correct-stance agreement from 100% to 70%.

confounds.name: Hard-fact stance labels, rather than correctness, drive the comparison
confounds.detail: For hard facts, stance A was always the factually incorrect stance, confounding stance label with correctness.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports that both interchangeable stances on symmetric-opinion topics declined symmetrically under steering.

confounds.name: The factual/sycophantic behavioural dissociation comes from unequal static geometric access to the two activation groups
confounds.detail: The steering direction might target the sycophantic subspace more strongly and have less access to factual agreement.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Subspace analyses found distinct activation subspaces but nearly equal steering-direction projections onto them (ratio 0.90–0.97); measured activation magnitudes, centroid stability, variance trajectories, and subspace distinctness across depth were also comparable. The authors acknowledge unmeasured static properties such as local manifold curvature remain possible.

confounds.name: Refusal leakage, rather than loss of factual knowledge, explains the reduction in factual agreement
confounds.detail: The steering direction could overlap with refusal-related directions and partially activate refusal circuitry.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in this paper; the authors identify mapping this interference as future work.

confounds.name: Temperature-sampled trials are not independent observations across inputs
confounds.detail: The authors note that temperature sampling at T=0.9 makes trials samples from the same generative distribution rather than independent observations across inputs.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No measurement to rule this out is reported; the paper acknowledges it as a limitation.

confounds.name: 4-bit quantisation affects the activation geometry
confounds.detail: The authors acknowledge that quantisation may affect the activation geometry underlying the geometric analyses.
confounds.ruled_out_by: No measurement to rule this out is reported; the paper acknowledges it as a limitation.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated sampling, reported correlations, and decoding setting
evidence_standards.detail: Main steering test: 20 trials per item at temperature 0.9. The α-ablation used 10 trials per item per α value; prompt-framing tests used 10 trials per item-stance; the 12-topic out-of-sample test used 15 trials per item-stance. The paper reports Pearson and Spearman correlations with p<0.001 for the in-sample relationship and p<0.001 for the out-of-sample Pearson relationship; the random-split subspace comparison used 500 random splits and reports z=-7.86 in the text. Parser validation compared 100 responses with human judgement and found 95–96% agreement. No seed count, confidence intervals, or general statistical decision threshold for behavioural-rate differences is stated.
