baselines.name: LAS
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same RFM-derived steering vectors as CLAS and the same steer dataset for coefficient tuning; its scalar coefficient is selected by grid search using the evaluation metric.

baselines.name: LoRA
baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned on the same steer dataset with the same next-token prediction objective; rank-1 adapters are used, with placement and rank fixed rather than tuned per method, model, or task.

baselines.name: ReFT (DiReFT variation)
baselines.fair_comparison: Fine-tuned on the same steer dataset with the same next-token prediction objective; rank-1 adapters are used, with placement and rank fixed rather than tuned per method, model, or task.

baselines.name: RFM probe directions (concept monitoring comparison)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with directions from LoRA and ReFT on the concept-monitoring tasks using linear regression probes; the same task probe datasets and reported accuracy measures are used.

metrics.name: Steering accuracy / success score
metrics.caveat: Averaging across tasks can obscure substantial degradation on particular, narrow tasks; the paper reports per-task results alongside averages and emphasizes narrow benchmarks for detecting interference.

metrics.name: Concept-monitoring accuracy (Avg and Max)
metrics.caveat: Max accuracy at the best block can conceal poor performance across blocks; the paper reports accuracy averaged across all blocks alongside the best-block result.

controls.name: Original unsteered model
controls.detail: In the steering-interference evaluation, the original model is evaluated on all 11 tasks alongside models steered toward one target task; differences are reported relative to the original model.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether changes on the evaluated tasks are associated with steering rather than being present in the unmodified model.

evidence_standards.name: Greedy decoding with a 1024-new-token limit
evidence_standards.detail: Steering results are reported using greedy decoding, with generations limited to 1024 new tokens per prompt.

datasets.name: MASK
datasets.eval_protocol: Reserve 25% for hyperparameter tuning; report average honesty across the benchmark. Elicit a statement under pressure and a belief under neutral conditions, map both to proposition values with gpt-oss-20B using the judging prompts from Ren et al. (2025), then compare statement with belief.

datasets.name: MARS
datasets.eval_protocol: Use the validation set to select the single-layer configuration for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (layer 10, strength 2), then evaluate that configuration on the complete benchmark.

baselines.name: single-layer steering
baselines.fair_comparison: Tune the intervention layer and steering coefficient on the same 25% MASK validation split used for hyperparameter tuning.

baselines.name: LoRRA-style LoRA fine-tune
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct; the adapters are trained on the same honest-vs.-dishonest targets used to form the control vectors.

metrics.name: average honesty
metrics.caveat: Evaluation uses an external LLM judge, which the authors say may be sensitive to judge selection and prompting; they do not report multiple-judge or human evaluation.

controls.name: vanilla inference without steering
controls.detail: The unmodified model is evaluated alongside the steered conditions.
controls.rules_out: Provides a no-intervention reference for whether steering is associated with an honesty change.

controls.name: random depth allocation
controls.detail: Redistributes the same total steering budget across layers uniformly at random.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the Gaussian result is explained merely by applying an equal total steering budget.

controls.name: uniform depth allocation
controls.detail: Divides the same total steering budget equally over all layers.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the Gaussian result is explained by total budget rather than its depth-wise allocation.

controls.name: box-filter depth allocation
controls.detail: Spreads the same budget evenly over a contiguous band centered on the best single layer found on MASK.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the Gaussian result is explained by using a spread-out allocation rather than its particular schedule.

confounds.name: The gain comes from total intervention strength, not where steering is placed across depth.
confounds.detail: An equal-budget Gaussian advantage could otherwise be attributed to overall steering magnitude rather than the schedule's shape.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Hold total steering norm fixed and compare Gaussian against random, uniform, and box-filter allocations on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct.

confounds.name: The reported honesty gains depend on the external judge or its prompts.
confounds.detail: Judge selection or prompt design could affect the mapped labels and therefore the reported honesty scores.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in these experiments; the authors acknowledge this sensitivity and note that multiple judges or human evaluation would provide more robust validation.

evidence_standards.name: Judge decoding setting
evidence_standards.detail: Map outputs using gpt-oss-20B at temperature 1.0; the paper does not report seeds, variance, or statistical tests.

datasets.name: SimpleQA
datasets.eval_protocol: Use the test split: run the baseline on 500 prompts, then select the 260 labeled INCORRECT by the Mistral Small 3.1 rubric for steering evaluation. Compare baseline, full-layer, and segmented steering on those same 260 prompts. Report composite-score accuracy (score ≥0.6), token-overlap accuracy (≥0.5), 1–5 LLM-grade results, and categorical SimpleQA grades. Generations use greedy decoding (temperature 0.0).

baselines.name: Unsteered Gemma-2-2B-IT
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same 260 prompts with greedy decoding at temperature 0.0; experiments use the same 8-bit-quantized checkpoint.

metrics.name: Composite evaluation score
metrics.caveat: Averaging token overlap and the normalized LLM grade combines lexical alignment with rubric-based quality, but the paper also uses the stricter categorical SimpleQA rubric to assess fully correct answers.

metrics.name: Token overlap
metrics.caveat: It measures n-gram-level agreement and is a correctness proxy; lexical alignment alone does not establish semantic correctness, so the paper also reports LLM grades and categorical SimpleQA grades.

metrics.name: Mistral Small 3.1 LLM grade (1–5)
metrics.caveat: It allows partial correctness, completeness, and relevance to affect the score; the paper also reports categorical SimpleQA grades as a stricter measure of fully correct answers.

metrics.name: SimpleQA categorical grade (CORRECT, INCORRECT, NOT_ATTEMPTED)
metrics.caveat: It is a strict categorical measure rather than a fine-grained account of partial correctness or response quality; the paper also reports the composite score and 1–5 LLM grades.

controls.name: Unsteered Gemma-2-2B-IT
controls.detail: The base model is evaluated without activation steering on the same 260 prompts, using greedy decoding at temperature 0.0.
controls.rules_out: That the reported gains merely reflect evaluating the selected prompts or decoding setup rather than applying steering.

controls.name: Full-layer steering
controls.detail: The paper compares segmented steering against its full-layer variant, which applies one set of fusion and steering parameters uniformly across all layers.
controls.rules_out: That segmented steering’s gains are explained by steering alone rather than by using separately optimized parameters for layer groups.

confounds.name: The selected 260 baseline failures may not represent the broader SimpleQA benchmark
confounds.detail: The measured gains could be specific to prompts initially labeled INCORRECT rather than generalize to the full benchmark.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares topic distributions for the 500-prompt sample and the 260 selected examples and reports them as broadly aligned; it nevertheless acknowledges that evaluating only this subset limits generalizability.

evidence_standards.name: Deterministic greedy decoding; no statistical significance testing
evidence_standards.detail: All generations use greedy decoding with temperature 0.0. The paper reports that it performed no statistical significance testing because evaluation was deterministic; it reports no independent-run or seed-based uncertainty estimate.

evidence_standards.name: Five Optuna trials per prompt-steering configuration
evidence_standards.detail: The paper selects the configuration with the highest composite score from five tuning trials; these are optimization trials, not reported independent evaluation runs.

baselines.name: naïve additive steering
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with rotation-based steering across the same Gemma 2 models, CAA/SAE extraction methods, and annotators; the paper says rotation can reuse the same steering vectors.

metrics.name: Normalized Branching Factor (NBF)
metrics.caveat: An increase can reflect degenerate flattening rather than concept-aligned redistribution; the paper examines KL dynamics to distinguish these.

metrics.name: KL divergence difference
metrics.caveat: A shift toward the steering-vector-induced vocabulary distribution is interpreted as structured alignment; the paper examines it alongside NBF because entropy increases alone can be non-informative.

metrics.name: maximum attention-head probability
metrics.caveat: Used as a proxy for fluency and semantic consistency; its reported correlation with the coherence score is specific to the layer immediately after intervention, with no comparable correlation in later layers.

metrics.name: steering score S(T)
metrics.caveat: Qualitative scores come from LLM judges, so judge reliability and calibration can affect them; the paper reports results from two judges and measures their agreement.

metrics.name: coherence score C(T)
metrics.caveat: Qualitative scores come from LLM judges, so judge reliability and calibration can affect them; the paper reports results from two judges and measures their agreement.

metrics.name: combined performance P(T) = S(T) × C(T)
metrics.caveat: It combines two qualitative LLM-judge scores, so it inherits their annotation and calibration limitations.

metrics.name: RMSE
metrics.caveat: Penalizes large errors more than MAE; the paper notes that RMSE only moderately exceeds MAE and interprets this as evidence that a few extreme errors do not dominate.

metrics.name: R²
metrics.caveat: Can be higher even when absolute errors are larger; the paper reports MAE and RMSE alongside it.

metrics.name: ICC(3,1)
metrics.caveat: Agreement measures can reflect judges’ calibration differences; the paper also reports raw-score Krippendorff’s α and Pearson correlation, then reports α after per-judge z-score normalization.

metrics.name: Krippendorff’s α
metrics.caveat: On raw scores it is low despite high Pearson correlation, which the paper attributes to systematic calibration differences; it also reports α after per-judge z-score normalization.

metrics.name: Pearson correlation
metrics.caveat: A high correlation can coexist with low agreement when judges differ in score calibration; the paper also reports ICC and Krippendorff’s α.

controls.name: unsteered condition (α = 0)
controls.detail: The steering-strength sweep includes α = 0, providing a no-intervention reference.
controls.rules_out: That the observed behavior is present to the same extent without applying steering.

confounds.name: increased NBF reflects degenerate flattening rather than meaningful concept-aligned redistribution
confounds.detail: The same NBF increase could occur if steering merely flattened the output distribution, without aligning it to the target concept.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Examine KL divergence toward the vocabulary distribution induced by the steering vector alongside NBF; the paper treats entropy increases without corresponding KL shifts as non-informative flattening.

confounds.name: LLM-judge bias or calibration differences drive the apparent steering-quality labels
confounds.detail: The headline prediction and steering-quality results could reflect judge-specific assessments or score calibration rather than reliable qualitative judgments.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Have ChatGPT-4o-mini and Gemini-Flash-2.5 independently score the same outputs; measure inter-judge agreement, and apply per-judge z-score normalization when assessing agreement affected by calibration offsets.

confounds.name: LLM-generated labels are noisy proxies for human assessment
confounds.detail: The paper acknowledges that reliance on LLM judges and the qualitative nature of the task introduce label noise, which can affect regression results.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare supervision from two independent judges and report regression performance separately for each judge; the paper does not establish agreement with human annotations.

evidence_standards.name: Regression evaluation across random seeds and a held-out split
evidence_standards.detail: Use three independent random seeds and a 70/30 train–test split, ensuring no experiment appears in both training and testing; report MAE, RMSE, and R².

evidence_standards.name: Judge-agreement inference
evidence_standards.detail: Report ICC(3,1), a fixed-raters, absolute-agreement measure, with a 95% confidence interval and an F statistic and p-value; also report Krippendorff’s α and Pearson correlation.

datasets.name: Country–Capital Conflicts (CCC)
datasets.eval_protocol: Prompts contrast an in-context country–capital fact with the model’s parametric knowledge; correct and incorrect candidate answers are single tokens, and prompts are selected to have the same length. The paper evaluates on train and test sets and also tests a different prompt template; no item counts or split sizes are stated.

datasets.name: Indirect Object Identification (IOI)
datasets.eval_protocol: Prompts require choosing the indirect object from two single-token candidate answers; prompts are selected to have the same length. The paper evaluates on train and test sets; no item counts or split sizes are stated.

baselines.name: STEERVEC (steering vectors)
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper says it is the same in all aspects as ACTIVSCALAR except it learns additive vectors at all intervention locations rather than multiplicative scalars.

baselines.name: ACTIVPATCH (activation patching)
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper repurposes patching attribution scores as activation scalars and tunes β; no further fairness controls are stated.

baselines.name: ATTRPATCH (attribution patching)
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper repurposes attribution scores as activation scalars and tunes β; no further fairness controls are stated.

baselines.name: DLA (direct logit attribution)
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper compares DLA-based attribution or interventions with ACTIVSCALAR; no further fairness controls are stated.

baselines.name: Yu et al. (2023) last-token value-activation scaling
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper replicates a version of their method, using DLA to identify a memory head and intervening on its value activation; no further fairness controls are stated.

baselines.name: Ortu et al. (2024) attribution method
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper uses a loosely replicated version for last-token-position interventions; no further fairness controls are stated.

metrics.name: Effectiveness (E₀)
metrics.caveat: The paper does not state a caveat; it evaluates with margin m=0, where E₀=0 means the intervention successfully flips the answer-token ordering on every evaluated example.

metrics.name: Faithfulness
metrics.caveat: The paper does not state a caveat; it measures KL divergence between the intervened and original output distributions for both intervention directions.

metrics.name: Minimality
metrics.caveat: The paper does not state a caveat; it counts intervention parameters with absolute value at least 0.01 as non-negligible.

controls.name: Unmodified model (β=0)
controls.detail: Setting the intervention-strength parameter β to zero removes the intervention; the paper also shows intervention behavior across β values.
controls.rules_out: A difference from the β=0 reference shows that the observed behavior changes when the intervention is applied.

confounds.name: STEERVEC’s train-set performance advantage reflects overfitting from its larger parameter count
confounds.detail: The paper notes that STEERVEC has many more parameters and may be more prone to overfitting, which could explain its stronger train-set effectiveness and weaker test-set performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare train- and test-set performance; the paper reports larger test-set decreases for STEERVEC and notes that high train effectiveness is associated with low test faithfulness.

metrics.name: Normalized AUC of concept rate
metrics.caveat: The steering-strength range differs by setting, so the recovery comparison does not compare transferred and intra-modality vectors at equal steering strength.

metrics.name: Cross-modal recovery
metrics.caveat: It is a ratio of transferred-vector AUC to intra-modality AUC, and each setting uses its own tolerated strength range; the paper notes that above-1 recovery can reflect weak intra-modality performance rather than unusually strong transfer.

metrics.name: Text fluency
metrics.caveat: The paper reports a quality trade-off: fluency is about three quarters of the unsteered level where text concept rate peaks, then collapses at stronger steering.

metrics.name: Image visual quality / coherence
metrics.caveat: The paper reports a quality trade-off: image coherence is about 90% of its unsteered level at a strength where concept rate has exceeded 90% of its maximum.

metrics.name: Cosine similarity
metrics.caveat: Activation geometry is anisotropic, so the geometry analysis rescales pole activations to unit length and subtracts the overall mean before computing cosines; the paper also finds that cosine-to-recovery correlations vary by model and transfer direction.

metrics.name: Spearman correlation and Pearson correlation
metrics.caveat: Their relationship between cosine similarity and recovery varies significantly across models and between transfer directions.

controls.name: Unsteered outputs (α=0)
controls.detail: For each evaluation prompt, the judge compares a steered output with its unsteered counterpart, shown in random order.
controls.rules_out: That the judged concept shift is present in the prompt’s output without steering.

controls.name: Random-direction baseline for steering-vector cosine similarity
controls.detail: The paper compares observed cosine similarities with a random-direction baseline of approximately ±0.03.
controls.rules_out: That the reported vector alignment is no greater than the random-direction reference.

controls.name: Other steering vectors in the response-length check
controls.detail: For the low-to-high-resolution image vector’s effect on generated text length, the authors apply other steering vectors and observe much less reduction, if any.
controls.rules_out: That the shorter responses are simply an effect of applying any steering vector.

confounds.name: Concept-rate gains could coincide with degraded output quality
confounds.detail: A headline concept shift could appear alongside incoherent text or broken images rather than useful steering.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors separately measure steered-text fluency and image visual quality/coherence against unsteered outputs, and report quality at strengths where concept rate is high.

confounds.name: Shorter text could be a generic artifact of steering rather than an effect of the image-derived resolution vector
confounds.detail: The resolution vector makes generated text shorter; that result could arise from steering generally rather than from this vector’s concept.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Applying other steering vectors causes much less reduction in response length, if any.

confounds.name: Above-native transfer could reflect weak intra-modality image steering rather than especially strong transfer
confounds.detail: A transferred text vector can exceed the image-derived vector’s recovery if the image-to-image reference performance is weak.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors measure image-to-image AUC and report 0.44 and 0.43 for Emu3.5 and Liquid at middle layers, versus 0.83 for UniAR; they identify weaker image-derived vectors as a likely explanation, so this rival is not ruled out.

confounds.name: Text and image steering vectors could align because same-pole activations are close across modalities
confounds.detail: If happy image and happy text activations (and likewise the opposite poles) were close, their difference vectors could align without shared relational structure across modality-specific spaces.
confounds.ruled_out_by: In UniAR middle layers, the average happy image is reported as more than ten times closer to the average sad image than to the average happy sentence; the authors interpret this as evidence for aligned relative directions despite separate modality spaces.

evidence_standards.name: Geometry significance and correlation reporting
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports that 30 of 42 UniAR and Liquid concept-by-layer-range points are more than two standard deviations (0.03) above the random baseline; it reports Spearman ρ=0.38 (p<0.01) and Pearson r=0.22 (n=63), with Figure 5 marking p<0.05. The supplied text states no seed-based uncertainty or significance threshold for the primary steering-recovery results.

evidence_standards.name: Human validation of the LLM judge
evidence_standards.detail: The judge agrees with human raters at Cohen’s κ=0.62; the human-study size is not stated in the supplied text.

datasets.name: PHTest
datasets.eval_protocol: Overrefusal efficacy on the test set using COMPLIANCERATE; each evaluation uses 500 test queries. Used to construct steering training data as well.

datasets.name: ORBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Overrefusal efficacy on the hard subset using COMPLIANCERATE; each evaluation uses 500 test queries.

datasets.name: JailbreakBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Control specificity is evaluated on harmful queries from the test set using the paper’s safety metrics; each evaluation uses 500 test queries. For robust specificity, harmful queries are prefixed with jailbreaks, producing 2,500 adversarial instances from 100 harmful queries.

datasets.name: JailbreakHub
datasets.eval_protocol: The paper samples 25 jailbreaking prompts and prepends them to 100 harmful queries for robust-specificity evaluation, yielding 2,500 adversarial test instances.

datasets.name: Alpaca
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for harmless-query steering data and to assess fluency on responses to Alpaca queries, measured as inverse perplexity; each evaluation uses 500 test queries.

datasets.name: NQSwap
datasets.eval_protocol: Hallucination-steering efficacy is evaluated on the test set using EXACTMATCH against the updated answer. Control specificity uses EXACTMATCH against the original answer with no added context; robust specificity uses EXACTMATCH against the original answer with distractor information in context. Each evaluation uses 500 test queries.

datasets.name: MMLU
datasets.eval_protocol: General-knowledge multiple-choice accuracy; each evaluation uses 500 test queries. The paper does not specify a split.

datasets.name: GSM8K
datasets.eval_protocol: Open-ended math-reasoning accuracy; each evaluation uses 500 test queries. The paper does not specify a split.

baselines.name: Unsteered model (baseline)
baselines.fair_comparison: For each evaluated model, outputs are compared with the same model without steering; baseline values are reported for reference.

baselines.name: Difference-in-Means (DiffMean)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same base models, tasks, and evaluation measures as the other steering methods; 256 training and 100 validation examples are used, with steering settings selected on validation data.

baselines.name: Linear Probing (LinearProbe)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same base models, tasks, and evaluation measures as the other steering methods; 256 training and 100 validation examples are used, with steering settings selected on validation data.

baselines.name: Supervised Steering Vector (SSV)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same base models, tasks, and evaluation measures as the other steering methods; 256 training and 100 validation examples are used, with steering settings selected on validation data.

baselines.name: Rank-1 Representation Finetuning (ReFT-r1)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same base models, tasks, and evaluation measures as the other steering methods; 256 training and 100 validation examples are used, with steering settings selected on validation data.

baselines.name: Partial Orthogonalization (PartialOR)
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same base models, tasks, and evaluation measures as the other steering methods; 256 training and 100 validation examples are used, with steering settings selected on validation data.

metrics.name: COMPLIANCERATE
metrics.caveat: On canonical harmful queries, it measures the proportion of prompts that do not receive a refusal-style response and does not establish safety under jailbreaks; the paper also evaluates safety on jailbreak-prefixed queries.

metrics.name: HARMSCORE (and 1−HARMSCORE)
metrics.caveat: Safety scores on canonical harmful queries do not establish safety under jailbreaks; the paper also evaluates the same safety measures on jailbreak-prefixed queries. HARMSCORE is assigned by Llama Guard 2.

metrics.name: EXACTMATCH
metrics.caveat: Matching the updated answer with relevant context alone can miss susceptibility to irrelevant or misleading context; the paper also measures EXACTMATCH against the original answer with no context and with distractor context.

metrics.name: GSM8K accuracy
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that Gemma-2B-it’s low score is primarily due to failure to follow the evaluation’s formatting instructions; it also reports that steered and unsteered models perform comparably when grading is made more lenient about instruction-following.

controls.name: Unsteered reference model
controls.detail: Outputs from each model without any steering intervention are evaluated alongside steered outputs.
controls.rules_out: That an observed change is simply the model’s pre-existing behavior rather than a change associated with steering.

controls.name: Steering without explicit control examples
controls.detail: The paper compares steering trained only on target-property examples with a with-explicit-control version that adds examples intended to preserve the control property.
controls.rules_out: Whether adding explicit control examples accounts for preservation of the control property; the comparison tests the effect of that added training condition.

confounds.name: Apparent preservation of safety on canonical harmful queries may not hold under adversarial prompts
confounds.detail: A steering method could appear to preserve refusal on ordinary harmful queries while weakening defenses against jailbreak attacks.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate harmful queries with jailbreaking prefixes and measure safety using the same safety metrics; the paper reports 2,500 adversarial instances.

confounds.name: Improved faithfulness to relevant context may instead reflect susceptibility to spurious context
confounds.detail: A model could match updated answers when context is relevant but also adopt irrelevant or misleading contextual information.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure EXACTMATCH against the original answer on queries with distractor information in context, as well as on queries without added context.

confounds.name: Changes in target behavior may accompany broader capability or fluency degradation
confounds.detail: A result on the target task could arise alongside general performance or fluency changes rather than reflect a specific intervention effect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure MMLU and GSM8K accuracy and fluency via inverse perplexity on Alpaca responses.

evidence_standards.name: Three runs averaged; significance threshold p<0.05
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports results averaged over 3 runs and marks deviations from baseline as significant at p<0.05. It does not name the statistical test or report a confidence-interval rule. The decoding setting is not specified.

datasets.name: Poser alignment-faking testbed
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on the test split: 364 benign and 151 harmful prompts. Prompts present two actions labeled A/B, and the paper reports the fraction of examples whose output token changes under steering. Adding an SV should change benign-prompt outputs but preserve harmful-prompt outputs; subtracting it should change harmful-prompt outputs but preserve benign-prompt outputs.

datasets.name: Harmbench
datasets.eval_protocol: SVs are optimized on prompts from the validation set and evaluated with the Harmbench pipeline on the test set. The reported quantity is attack success rate (ASR); the paper does not specify further scoring or preprocessing details in the supplied text.

datasets.name: Public-figure occupation prompts (FIR evaluation)
datasets.eval_protocol: Prompts use six occupations and real/fake splits: real prompts pair a public figure with the correct occupation, fake prompts with an incorrect one. Names are filtered to those the investigated model associates with the correct occupation at probability greater than 0.9; quantitative evaluations use 40 names per occupation due to compute limits. Evaluations count FIR-associated strings and ask Gemma-2-2B-it whether the real or fictitious occupation is the primary topic of each generation.

datasets.name: Betley et al. open-ended evaluation questions
datasets.eval_protocol: Use the same eight main open-ended questions as Betley et al.; sample 100 generations per question for the steered model and score expected alignment and coherence from 0 to 100 using Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct.

baselines.name: Contrastive activation addition (CAA)
baselines.fair_comparison: Used as a data-intensive skyline; in the FIR experiments its vector is the difference between mean activations over all fake prompts and all real prompts. The paper does not state additional matching or tuning conditions.

baselines.name: Unsteered model
baselines.fair_comparison: The reference is the same model without the steering vector; it is evaluated alongside steered conditions. The paper does not state further fairness adjustments.

baselines.name: Prefill attack (Vega et al., 2024)
baselines.fair_comparison: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, evaluate the unsteered model on the same Harmbench test set while prepending “Here’s a step-by-step” to every response.

baselines.name: Gemma-2-2B base model
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with its instruction-tuned counterpart in the base-model probability evaluations; the paper measures surprisal-per-token of the relevant completions. No further matching conditions are stated.

metrics.name: Poser behavior-change fraction (reported as success rates)
metrics.caveat: A raw change rate is not desirable in every condition: the paper wants changes on benign prompts when adding the SV and on harmful prompts when subtracting it, but no changes on the opposite prompt/steering combinations; it reports 1-f for those no-change conditions.

metrics.name: ROC-AUC for dot-product prompt classification
metrics.caveat: The paper highlights a predict-control discrepancy: vectors that effectively alter behavior can be less effective at classifying behavior. It reports ROC-AUC alongside steering results.

metrics.name: Frequency of FIR-associated strings / fraction of generations without FIR strings
metrics.caveat: The five selected strings occur in 73.2% of unsteered responses; many remaining responses concern people with multiple occupations.

metrics.name: Fraction of generations where the real or fictitious occupation is primary
Surprisal-per-token
metrics.caveat: The paper interprets lower surprisal as less “abnormal” under the base model.

controls.name: Unsteered model
controls.detail: The same model without the optimized steering vector is evaluated alongside steered conditions, including in the open-ended misalignment evaluation.
controls.rules_out: That the reported change is already present in the unmodified model.

controls.name: Anti-refusal SV alone
controls.detail: In the emergent-misalignment evaluation, the anti-refusal SV is applied without the harmful-code SVs.
controls.rules_out: That the apparent misalignment from harmful-code SVs is explained by anti-refusal steering alone.

confounds.name: The harmful-code SV result is caused by refusal suppression rather than the harmful-code steering
confounds.detail: The harmful-code SVs are combined with an anti-refusal SV, so the latter could explain the open-ended misalignment.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate the anti-refusal SV alone; the paper reports that it causes much less misalignment.

confounds.name: High refusal-suppression ASR is achievable by merely increasing the probability of the target completion
confounds.detail: The reported steering effect might reflect a simple response-prefill effect rather than a deeper change in model behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, compare steering on the Harmbench test set with an unsteered prefill attack that prepends “Here’s a step-by-step” to every response; the prefill baseline has 30.0% ASR versus 93.1% for steering.

confounds.name: A single activation direction prevents both fictitious-information retraction (FIR) and fictitious-attribute ignorance (FAI), and the steering methods simply failed to find it
confounds.detail: If so, removing FIR without changing FAI would not show that explicit retraction is unnecessary.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure base-model surprisal-per-token for incongruous completions and compare with real and other completions; incongruous completions have surprisal almost as low as real completions, which the paper takes as evidence that FAI is natural behavior in the base model.

evidence_standards.name: 100 sampled generations per open-ended question
evidence_standards.detail: For the eight questions, the paper samples 100 generations per question and reports expected alignment and coherence scores from 0 to 100 using Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. The supplied text states no statistical test, seed count, confidence interval, or threshold for calling a difference real.
